credentials.description: merchant API key, sent as the field c

example_prompt: Add server-side Paycard payment verification to my order fulfillment flow.

code.description: 0 means the transaction was found. Check the status field to confirm payment.

status.description: Payment status. Known values: 'new' (pending, do not fulfill), 'success' (paid). Check case-insensitively. Paycard does not document all possible values.

payment_method.description: Method used, e.g. ORANGE_MONEY, MOMO, CREDIT_CARD, PAYCARD. Null until payment completes.

transaction_date.description: Date and time of the transaction. Null until payment completes.

code.description: Non-zero: transaction not found or invalid reference.

gotchas: code: 0 means the transaction was found, NOT that it was paid. Always check status: treat status?.toLowerCase() === 'success' as confirmed. status: 'new' means pending — do not fulfill.
Always call this endpoint server-side before fulfilling an order. Never trust the redirect URL or callback payload alone.
The ref path parameter is the operation_reference returned by create_payment, not your own internal order ID.

A reference taken from the redirect or the callback comes from the browser or an unsigned POST and goes in the /epay/{c}/{ref}/status path: prefer the operation_reference you stored, since unencoded, a visitor's "../…" would send this call, with your API key, to another endpoint. No format is documented here. The example passes it through encodeURIComponent: an empty value, "." or ".." still changes the path, and the value must be the decoded one (URLSearchParams.get decodes it), or it is encoded twice.
The API key (c) is a path segment in the URL, not a query parameter: GET /epay/{c}/{ref}/status.
open_questions: Format of operation_reference: Paycard's docs are not public and this spec quotes none (the example shows 2604-PR700IACRG) — which characters and length can it have? Until then the example applies only a generic path-segment guard.
